title: Institutions and transformative change in water management: A case study of wetland restoration on the island of Öland, Sweden
content:
by Cora Cunningham, Erik Andersson, Malgorzata Blicharska, Carolin Seiferth, Maria Tengö, Wiebren Johannes Boonstra

Institutions play a dual role in sustainability transformations. On the one hand, they may impede transformative change by reproducing views, structures, and practices that either contribute to environmental damage or fail to effectively address such damage. On the other hand, they are also needed to institutionalise new views and practices that enable transformation and the restructuring of society towards sustainability. In this paper, we take a closer look at the dual role of institutions in relation to transformative change through a case study of wetland restoration on the Swedish island of Öland. A key institution for water management in Sweden are so-called ‘drainage enterprises’. As the name suggests, these institutions were originally established to drain water from land for cultivation purposes. While land use and its values have changed considerably on Öland over the past 150 years, the legal status of drainage enterprises has remained intact. Today, this legal status hampers efforts to retain water on land, including wetland restoration. Results from the case study are used to discuss the relation of institutions to sustainability transformations, and what this means in practice for pursuing transformative change in water management, especially during times when the legitimacy and confidence in public institutions stands under pressure.
author: Cora Cunningham
